intro.title:

intro.lede: MARVI puts groundwater science in the hands of the people who depend on it—farmers, schools, researchers and communities working together for water that lasts!

blocks.quote: How can a village understand an invisible shared resource—and decide its future together?

blocks.title: The MARVI 4-S Strategy
blocks.lede: MARVI brings technical knowledge, community experience and practical monitoring together at village level.

items.title: Sense
items.text:
Measure groundwater levels, rainfall, water quality and recharge structures with simple field tools.  Farmers, Bhujal Jaankaars and local citizens regularly measure groundwater levels, rainfall and other local water conditions to build a shared understanding of their groundwater system.

Upload observations to MyWell and turn repeated measurements into understandable trends.

items.title: Store
items.text: Capture and recharge more water locally. Communities identify practical ways to improve groundwater recharge, including farm-scale and community recharge interventions, such as  pits, ponds, check-dams  suited to local conditions.

items.title: Share
items.text:
Share groundwater more fairly and efficiently. 
Communities explore cooperative approaches to groundwater use, including sharing groundwater between farmers, so more people benefit from available water.
Also, share learning and experiences with others for a better groundwater future in the region.

items.title: Sustain
items.text: Use groundwater within its long-term limits. Monitoring, recharge and collective decision-making help communities balance groundwater use with replenishment and protect the resource for the future.

blocks.title: The village’s own groundwater champions.
blocks.lede: “Groundwater informed”: local volunteers who connect careful observation with community knowledge and collective action.

photo.alt: A Bhujal Jankaar measuring a village well

right.lead: A Bhujal Jankaar makes groundwater science legible—well by well, season by season, village by village.
paragraphs: These trained volunteers measure wells, rainfall, water quality and check dams. They interpret local patterns, explain them in the community’s own language and help farmers see that groundwater is both limited and shared.

features.title: Measure consistently
features.text: Build a trustworthy local record through simple, repeated observations.

features.title: Interpret locally
features.text: Connect readings with crops, rainfall, pumping and village experience.

features.title: Communicate openly
features.text: Take groundwater information into schools, meetings and farm decisions.

features.title: Support cooperation
features.text: Help communities discuss recharge, demand and fair use together.

blocks.title: Science becomes useful when it becomes local.
blocks.lede: The aim is to improve irrigation-water security and rural livelihoods by making the invisible visible.

items.title: Participatory monitoring
items.text: A groundwater-monitoring programme operated and understood by the village itself.

items.title: Recharge that can be measured
items.text: Assess rainwater-harvesting structures and understand what genuinely reaches the aquifer.

items.title: Decisions made together
items.text: Turn readings into conversations about crops, pumping, sharing and long-term water security.

blocks.title: From 10–15 metres in the 1960s to 30–40 metres today.
blocks.lede: In some places, farmers drill beyond 100 metres chasing a falling watertable. Recharge helps, but sustainable use also requires understanding demand.

items.title: The aquifer is shared
items.text: Water pumped from one well can affect neighbours drawing from the same underground store.

items.title: Rainfall is not recharge
items.text: Only part of rain reaches groundwater; soils, geology, land use and structures shape the journey.

items.title: Trends need time
items.text: A single reading is a snapshot. Repeated measurements reveal depletion, recovery and seasonal rhythm.
